t: Your unpaid second job at the checkout
d: You scan it, bag it and fix the unexpected item. Consumer NZ says the staff savings are not being passed on to shoppers.
b: You scan it. You bag it. You fix the "unexpected item in the bagging area". You wait in line to do it. None of that comes off your bill. How big self-checkout has become In 2023, around one in four Foodstuffs South Island purchases went through self-service, and over half at one Christchurch New World, 1News reported. [2] Who keeps the saving Supermarkets save on staff, and "those savings are not currently being passed on to shoppers." That is Consumer NZ, speaking to RNZ. [1] What shoppers and staff say 66% of Kiwis prefer a cashier over self-service, a Canstar Blue survey found in 2019. [3] In the 2026 Workers First retail staff survey, workers linked understaffing to more safety incidents, and more staff was the top fix they asked for. [4] Overseas, some are going back UK chain Booths removed self-checkouts from all but two stores from November 2023, and later reported less theft and faster service. [5] A 2024 Drexel University study found shoppers who use self-checkout for bigger baskets (more than 15 items) are less loyal to the store. [6] Our view Opinion, Guy Hollister, Shelf Audit: If you are doing the work, you should share the saving. Cramped bagging areas and long self-serve queues are a choice the store makes, and the shopper pays for it in time.

t: The duopoly, in the regulator's own words
d: In 2022 the Commerce Commission found competition between Woolworths and Foodstuffs was muted and their profits were well above normal.
b: This is not a conspiracy theory. It is the finding of a 609-page government market study. What the Commerce Commission found in March 2022 Woolworths NZ and Foodstuffs "operated effectively as a duopoly" in a $22 billion a year industry. [1][2] Competition between them was "muted". [2] Average returns on capital from 2015 to 2019 were 12.7% (Woolworths), 12.8% (Foodstuffs South Island) and 13.1% (Foodstuffs North Island). A normal return was estimated at 5.5%. [1] NZ grocery prices "appear relatively high by international standards". [1] "About $1 million a day" The then Commerce Minister, David Clark, described the sector as making excess profits of around $1 million a day. [3] That was the Government's summary of the excess return, not a daily accounting profit. Four years on The Commission's 2025 Annual Grocery Report, published 2 June 2026, says the major retailers still hold 82% of the market, an HHI of 3,585 shows "limited competitive pressure", and both Foodstuffs co-ops "sit at the top end of international profitability benchmarks". [4] Opinion: Two companies, four years of reform, the same 82%. Read the full share chart on our Who controls NZ page.

t: Specials that were not special: the court cases
d: Two Pak'nSaves have been convicted and fined $580,500. Woolworths faces criminal charges it has pleaded not guilty to.
b: On 30 October 2026, Pak'nSave Silverdale and Pak'nSave Mill Street were fined a combined $580,500 in the Auckland District Court after pleading guilty to inaccurate pricing under the Fair Trading Act. [1] Silverdale: $234,000 for 10 charges. Mill Street: $346,500 for 8 charges. [1] The charges included Pams Value white bread advertised at $1.15 but charged at $1.19, tissues shown at $2 but charged at $3, and Vogel's bread promoted as "extra low" when it was dearer than at any point in the past 2 years. [2] Woolworths The Commission filed criminal charges against Woolworths NZ in May 2025. It alleges that between January 2022 and September 2024, advertised prices did not match checkout prices, and some specials were not genuine. [3] Woolworths has pleaded not guilty while it seeks more detail, and says it has 3.5 million transactions a week and refunds overcharges in full. [4] These are allegations, not findings. Fines that fit The maximum fine today is $600,000 per charge. The Commission says proposed law changes would allow up to $5 million per breach. [5] Consumer NZ research found 62% of supermarket shoppers noticed pricing errors in the past year. [2] Opinion: Check your receipt. Every time.

t: Same chain, same product, different price
d: Our 1 November 2026 capture: 50.5% of 426 NZ supermarkets price above the national median. All 125 New World stores do.
b: Shelf Audit compares the same products across every store we can price. Here is what the capture of 1 November 2026 shows. [1] 426 priced supermarkets nationwide. 215 stores (50.5%) price above the national median. 211 (49.5%) are at or below it. The 215 above the median are on average 2.5% dearer, ranging from 0.1% to 6.6% over. The 211 at or below average 3.0% cheaper. All 125 New World stores we priced sit above the median, with price indexes from 101.4 to 106.6. What that means Two stores with the same logo can charge different prices for the same item. Which store you walk into changes your bill. Opinion: Higher prices are a choice. Look up your nearest stores on the Shelf Audit watchdog .

t: Shrinkflation: same price, less in the pack
d: Consumer NZ has tracked packs that shrank while the price stayed put, from rice crackers to chocolate boxes.
b: The price tag is the same. The pack is smaller. Consumer NZ has documented examples on NZ shelves. [1][2] Snickers LCMs: 132g down to 100g. [1] Peckish rice crackers: 100g down to 90g. [1] Cadbury Favourites boxes: 373g to 340g, and 570g to 520g. [3] Shrinkflation is usually a manufacturer's decision, not the supermarket's. But it is the supermarket shelf where it lands. Your defence: the unit price Since 31 August 2024, large NZ grocery stores must show a unit price (per kg, per litre) on regulated products. It must be clear and at least 25% of the size of the main price. [4] Compare per kg, not per pack.

t: Loyalty cards: you pay with your data
d: Everyday Rewards and Clubcard collect detailed purchase data. Consumer NZ warns member pricing can leave non-members paying more.
b: Member prices look like a gift. Consumer NZ says the trade is your data. [1] Woolworths' Everyday Rewards and New World's Clubcard collect detailed purchase and behaviour data, which can be shared with partners and used for targeted ads, Consumer NZ reports. [1] Consumer NZ warns member-only pricing can disadvantage shoppers without a card, an app or internet access. [2] It has not found individualised pricing in NZ, but says the data could make it possible. [3] What the regulator said The 2022 market study found the major chains' promotions, price labelling and loyalty schemes make it harder to compare prices over time and between stores. [4]

t: Home brands: the supermarket owns the shelf and the label
d: Private label is about 14.5% of packaged supermarket sales. The retailer sets the price of its own brand and its rivals'.
b: Private label (Pams, Woolworths brand and others) was about 14.5% of pre-packaged supermarket sales, per Circana data cited by the Commerce Commission. [1] Suppliers often make both their own brand and the supermarket's private label, chosen by tender. [1][2] The Commission says its monitoring found no evidence of preferential treatment for private label, but that monitoring covered only a small number of range reviews. [1] Opinion: When one company owns the shelf, sets the shelf price and owns one of the brands on it, shoppers deserve to see who made what. Shelf Audit is mapping brand owners next.

t: How suppliers are treated, and the code meant to fix it
g: Suppliers Grocery Supply Code Commerce Commission
d: Rebates and payments from suppliers hit about $6 billion in FY25. Both big groups have had Grocery Supply Code warnings.
b: In 2022 the Commission found the major groups use buying power to shift costs and risks onto suppliers. [1] Rebates, discounts and payments between the major retailers and suppliers were worth about $6 billion in FY25, 26% of their combined sales revenue. [2] In a 2024 survey of 562 suppliers, 35% rated their experience with Foodstuffs North Island negative or very negative, against 19% for Woolworths and 17% for Foodstuffs South Island. [3] In July 2025 the Commission warned Foodstuffs North Island it had likely breached the Grocery Supply Code by obstructing and delaying a supplier's request. [4] In December 2025 it warned Woolworths for likely failing to tell suppliers of their right to a review of delisting decisions. [5] A warning is the Commission's view of a likely breach, not a court finding.

t: 190 land deals that kept rivals out
d: The Commission found 190 covenants and exclusivity clauses blocking competitor sites. 150 lasted more than 20 years. Parliament banned them.
b: A supermarket needs a site. In 2022 the Commerce Commission found the two major groups had used covenants and lease clauses to stop sites going to competitors. [1][2] More than 190 restrictive and exclusivity covenants were identified. [2] 150 of them restricted sites for more than 20 years. [3] The Commission named a lack of suitable sites as one of the biggest barriers for new competitors, and recommended monitoring land banking. [1] The fix The Commerce (Grocery Sector Covenants) Amendment Act 2022 makes these grocery covenants prohibited and unenforceable. [4]

t: When a Pak'nSave is told not to discount
d: The Commission is suing Foodstuffs South Island, alleging it restricted its own Pak'nSaves from cutting prices. Foodstuffs NI faces a separate cartel case.
b: In August 2026 the Commerce Commission announced civil proceedings against Foodstuffs South Island. It alleges the co-op restricted independently owned Pak'nSave stores from discounting selected products without approval, under its "Super Deal" and "Every Day Low Price" rules, which the Commission says is resale price maintenance under section 37 of the Commerce Act. [1] The Commission also has proceedings against Foodstuffs North Island and liquor wholesaler Gilmours alleging cartel conduct. [2] Both cases are allegations before the courts. Nothing has been proven. Opinion: If the allegation is right, a shop wanted to charge you less and was not allowed to. Watch this case.

t: The price of not going in: delivery fees
d: Woolworths lifted its Delivery Saver fee and the free delivery threshold from $80 to $100 in October 2025.
b: From 1 October 2025, Woolworths' Delivery Saver went from $23 to $25.99 a month, and from $118 to $132.99 for six months. [1] The minimum order for free delivery rose from $80 to $100. [1] Online is now 8% of the major retailers' sales, and click and collect outsells delivery, the Commission reports. [2] Opinion: A higher threshold nudges a bigger basket. Price your delivery fee into your shop.

t: It's not just groceries: liquor and pharmacy
d: Foodstuffs supermarkets sell 20% of all NZ liquor and it owns Liquorland. Two chains lead pharmacy.
b: 20% of all NZ liquor is sold through Foodstuffs supermarkets, and Foodstuffs also owns Liquorland and the wholesalers Gilmours and Trents. [1] The two supermarket groups sell over 60% of beer, wine and cider. [2] Pharmacy: the Green Cross Health network (Unichem and Life Pharmacy) had 328 stores at 31 March 2025, and Chemist Warehouse about 70 at the end of 2025. [3][4] See every slice and its source on Who controls NZ .

t: The law that was meant to fix it
d: The Grocery Industry Competition Act 2023 created a Grocery Commissioner. Three annual reports later, the 82% has not moved.
b: The Grocery Industry Competition Act 2023 came into force on 10 July 2023. It created a Grocery Commissioner inside the Commerce Commission and a wholesale regime requiring the majors to consider supply requests from rivals. [1][2] The 2025 Annual Grocery Report says "little observable change" in core competition metrics, with the majors on 82%. [3] The Commission has said cost rises should not be "used as an opportunity to widen margins", and prices should come down quickly when costs fall. [4] Opinion: Watchdogs need data. That is why Shelf Audit prices every store.
